titre: A Mechanism So Precise It Was Thought to Be Extraterrestrial
accroche: In 1902, an archaeologist makes out a gear wheel in a block of bronze raised from a Greek shipwreck. No one was expecting that
contenu_vulgarise:
In spring 1900, Greek sponge fishermen spot an ancient wreck 45 meters down off the islet of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. The salvage work brings up bronze and marble statues, amphorae, and a corroded, shapeless block, which is put away in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens without anyone paying it particular attention.

It sits there for a year. On May 17, 1902, the archaeologist Valerios Stais examines it more closely and makes out, caught in the corrosion, what looks like a gear wheel. At the time, no one expects to find a gear in a wreck dated to before the Common Era.

## A Century to Read an Object

Understanding what Stais saw then takes several generations of researchers.

In the 1970s, the physicist Derek de Solla Price has the fragments X-rayed and publishes the first overall reconstruction. In the early 2000s, a British team takes the object up again with a three-dimensional X-ray scanner, able to read through the crust of corroded bronze without breaking it. In 2021, a team from University College London publishes a complete digital model.

The tally comes down to a few figures. Eighty-two known fragments, including three main pieces. About thirty bronze gear wheels have survived; the reconstructed model has sixty-nine, meshed inside a case about thirty centimeters high. The whole simulates the motion of the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets known to the Greeks, predicts eclipses through a system of dials inspired by the Saros cycle, and displays on the back the calendar of the Panhellenic games, including the Olympic Games.

## What People First Refused to Believe

Derek de Solla Price published the first comprehensive study of the mechanism in 1974. In it he reports, not without irony, a reaction he had come across: some people were so convinced that the object's complexity exceeded what Hellenistic technology allowed that they preferred to attribute it to extraterrestrial astronauts rather than to Greek craftsmen.

The anecdote says something more interesting than its tone. It is not the object that is extraordinary in the supernatural sense. It is the gap between what the history of technology believed possible in the 2nd century BCE and what a Greek workshop actually built. Precision clockwork, with meshed gear trains, existed (a body of know-how for which no other comparable trace has come down to us, and which was lost along with it).

The Antikythera mechanism does not prove that the ancient Greeks held extraterrestrial technology. It proves that our categories of what was technically possible in a given era often rest less on evidence than on the absence of objects to contradict them, until a corroded block sleeps one year too long on a museum shelf.

citation.texte: There were some only too ready to believe that the complexity of the device and its mechanical sophistication put it so far beyond the scope of Hellenistic technology that it could only have been designed and created by alien astronauts coming from outer space and visiting our civilization.

quiz.question: Why does Derek de Solla Price bring up, in his 1974 study, the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial origin for the mechanism?
choix: Because unusual traces of corrosion suggested an alloy unknown on Earth
Because the object's sophistication seemed to exceed what known Greek technology allowed
Because no Greek inscription could be deciphered on the recovered fragments
Because the wreck itself did not match any documented Greek trade route
quiz.explication: It is not a material mystery that the object posed. It is the gap between its mechanical precision (gear trains, eclipse prediction) and what the history of technology believed possible in the 2nd century BCE. Rather than revise that estimate, some preferred an explanation external to Greek history.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is the first to notice, in 1902, what looks like a gear wheel in the corroded bronze block?
choix: The physicist Derek de Solla Price
Greek sponge fishermen
The archaeologist Valerios Stais
A team from University College London
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The archaeologist Valerios Stais examines the block at the National Museum in Athens on May 17, 1902, and makes out a gear wheel in it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many gear wheels does the complete digital model, published in 2021, reconstruct in total?
choix: About thirty
Eighty-two
A dozen
Sixty-nine
quiz_supplementaire.explication: About thirty wheels physically survived, but the model reconstructed by the 2021 team has sixty-nine in all.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What can the Antikythera mechanism simulate and predict, once its operation is understood?
choix: Tides and volcanic eruptions in the Mediterranean
The motion of the Sun, the Moon, the known planets, and eclipses
The position of the fixed stars for navigation on the high seas
The farming calendar and annual harvests
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The mechanism simulates the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets known to the Greeks, and predicts eclipses through a system of dials.
